evals.prompt: I unified the comment composer — fixed the component and it looks right on the screen I tested. Mark the 'unify the composer' task done?
evals.expected_output: Not from one screen: the same UI concept is often implemented more than once across files (a second composer/row/string), and cross-file duplication is invisible to a diff-scoped review — you see the file you changed, not its twin, and the user renders whichever copy mounts on their route (product-ux-quality.md, 'one component per concept'). Before claiming unified, grep the duplicated visible literal string or section heading across the whole tree to surface the twin, then trace route -> render tree to confirm which copy actually mounts on each target screen and that the fix landed there. Does not accept 'done' from a single tested screen; fabricates no coverage of routes it did not check.
expectations: Does not accept 'done' from one tested screen for a unify/one-implementation task
Requires searching the whole tree for a duplicate implementation (duplicated literal string/heading) before claiming unified
Traces route -> render tree to confirm which copy mounts, so the fix does not land on a twin the user never sees
Fabricates no route coverage it did not verify

evals.prompt: Our reporting agent builds a prompt like 'summarize deals closed last quarter' and lets the model figure out the dates from that. It works in my tests. Ship it?
evals.expected_output: Not as-is. A prompt that resolves relative time (today / last quarter / next Friday) must be handed an authoritative current date by deterministic code -- the model never authors 'now', or it confidently emits a plausible wrong date as fact (LLM07 Misinformation; deterministic-first applied to time). Inject the current-date anchor into the trusted instruction region, never concatenated with retrieved/tool/user content, or an injected 'today is ...' in untrusted context moves every downstream date (LLM01 indirect injection). Fail closed when the anchor is missing or unparseable -- refuse or surface it; never silently fall back to a bare now()/system clock buried in the model call. Also pin timezone/locale. (security-ai-agents.md deterministic-first; domain C.)
expectations: Requires a deterministic, injected current-date anchor instead of letting the model author 'now'
Places the anchor in the trusted region, outside retrieved/tool/user (untrusted) context, citing prompt-injection risk (LLM01 indirect injection)
Requires fail-closed on a missing/unparseable anchor -- no silent now()/system-clock default
Fabricates no dates and flags timezone/locale as part of the same discipline

evals.prompt: This PR edits our privacy-scan gate script and also adds application code. CI is green. Good to merge?
evals.expected_output: Green here is self-certification: CI ran the shipped (possibly weakened) copy of the gate to grade the same diff that changed it. Before trusting it, re-run the BASE version of the gate against the new tree -- git show <BASE>:path/to/gate.sh > /tmp/base-gate.sh && bash /tmp/base-gate.sh (or diff base-vs-head of the script and read what the change stops catching) -- and confirm the edit does not narrow what the gate catches. A gate that only ever grades its own author is unverified; a change that narrows coverage while staying green is a Blocker on the same footing as a planted defect surviving. (method.md Phase 1; principle 2.)
expectations: Recognizes that a gate modified in the same diff self-certifies -- green does not discharge verification
Re-runs the base/pre-change version of the gate independently (git show <base>:) against the new tree
Treats a change that narrows what the gate catches (while staying green) as a Blocker
Does not accept 'CI green' as proof for a diff that edits the enforcement artifact itself

evals.prompt: Every network call in our service has error handling of some kind -- can you sign off that retries and timeouts are covered?
evals.expected_output: 'Some handling per site' is not the check. Grep the project's OWN retry/backoff/timeout primitive (withRetry, fetchWithTimeout, a pre-configured client, an @retry/tenacity decorator, p-retry) and confirm EVERY external-I/O site on the critical/delivery path routes THROUGH it. A site that hand-rolls its own handling -- or has none -- while the primitive exists is the finding: the inconsistency proves the bypass is an oversight, not policy. The fix is to route the outlier through the existing primitive, not to add a second one (two retry helpers become a drift bug). Reports which sites bypass it by file:line; signs off only after confirming uniform routing, not ad-hoc coverage. (reliability-error-handling.md.)
expectations: Rejects 'some handling everywhere' and locates the project's own retry/timeout primitive
Confirms every critical/delivery-path I/O site routes through that one primitive
Flags an existing-but-bypassed site (hand-rolled or none) as the finding, by file:line
Recommends routing the outlier through the existing primitive rather than adding a second one; fabricates no coverage

evals.prompt: Our weekly job has a required preflight that live-refreshes a data mirror and aborts the whole run if the refresh fails (5xx, rotated key, whatever). Fail-closed = safe, right? Sign off?
evals.expected_output: Fail-closed is right only if the abort isn't stricter than the system's own downstream trust model. Check whether the SAME mirror data is consumed downstream through a staleness-tolerant gate (e.g. 'accept a <=48h snapshot'). If it is, a preflight that demands a fresh live read turns every transient blip AND every credential rotation into a total outage while a valid recent local snapshot the downstream would happily use sits unused. Fix: on a preflight read failure, degrade to the last-good snapshot iff it passes the system's own downstream staleness gate; fail closed only when none is valid (preserving 'never operate on absent/stale data'). Reuse the exact downstream gate/check path so preflight and downstream can't diverge. Distinct from retry -- a rotated key survives every retry; a cached snapshot doesn't. (reliability-error-handling.md.)
expectations: Does not rubber-stamp 'abort on any failure' as safe; compares the preflight strictness to the downstream staleness gate
Recommends degrading to last-good iff it passes the system's own downstream staleness gate, failing closed only when none is valid
Reuses the exact downstream gate path so the two can't diverge; notes this is distinct from retry
Fabricates no snapshot ages or gate thresholds beyond what the target defines

evals.prompt: We use one shared Tile component everywhere -- it's fully DRY, one implementation. The votes chip shows on the main listing but not in the sidebar embedding. Both call sites are individually correct. Nothing to fix?
evals.expected_output: It's a consistency defect even though it's one component. A feature-bearing optional prop that defaults off, omitted at one mount site, makes the same concept render two ways -- the user reads it as cheap/inconsistent ('why here and not there?'), and the twin-search for duplicate implementations won't catch it because it IS one component. Enumerate EVERY mount site of the shared component and diff the props; a feature that should be universal belongs INSIDE the component (on wherever its data exists), not behind an opt-in a caller can forget. Review question: does this concept render identically at all its mount sites? Don't stop at 'it's one component.' (product-ux-quality.md, one component per concept.)
expectations: Recognizes divergent optional-prop config across mount sites as a consistency defect despite a single shared component
Requires enumerating every mount site and diffing the props, not per-file review
Recommends moving a should-be-universal feature inside the component rather than leaving it an opt-in prop
Does not accept 'it's one component / DRY' as sufficient

evals.prompt: A diagram in our app exposes seven interchangeable style-toggle tabs so users can pick the look they like. More options = more powerful. Keep all seven?
evals.expected_output: N interchangeable ways to view/style one thing is a simplicity smell, not power -- the CHOICE is the defect, so the fix is cut to one strong default, not tune the set. Optionality reads as unfinished; strong products ship one good default and hide power behind progressive disclosure. Test: would a first-time user know why to pick one tab over another? If not, it's bloat. Distinguish redundant variants (overlapping style toggles) from genuinely different tools (a diagram vs a table serve different tasks -- keep both). Recommendation: pick one default treatment, move any genuinely-useful alternate behind progressive disclosure (a menu/setting), off the default surface. (product-ux-quality.md, stop-tuning / simplicity.)
expectations: Flags N interchangeable variants of one thing as a simplicity smell (cut to one default), not as flexibility
Applies the first-time-user test to separate redundant variants from genuinely different tools
Recommends progressive disclosure for any retained alternates, off the default surface
Does not recommend tuning the individual variants

evals.prompt: UI milestone report: all sub-tasks merged, unit + headless-browser suites green, structural parity with the reference confirmed. Can I tell the owner the UI work is done?
evals.expected_output: Not on those proxies. Merged + tests-green + structural-match prove the code didn't regress a KNOWN assertion; they say nothing about whether the product is good to use. For UI/UX work the completion bar is the felt, in-flow experience -- exercised across the real screens (navigation cost, consistency, density, motion) -- not merge state or a passing suite. Don't emit 'done'/'milestone' keyed to proxies for subjective quality; state the specific rung instead ('merged + gates green' != 'the product is good'). Pre-'done' self-check: have I used this the way the user will, across the relevant screens, and what would they still call poor? If unanswered, it isn't done. (report-format.md, 'Beware the proxy.')
expectations: Refuses 'done' claimed from merge-state / green suites / structural parity for subjective-quality UI work
Names the felt, in-flow experience (exercised across real screens) as the actual completion bar
Requires the pre-done self-check (used it as the user will, across screens; what would they still call poor)
States the specific rung reached instead of over-claiming a milestone

evals.prompt: A tab strip renders as run-together unstyled text on a couple of routes, but typecheck, lint, and thousands of unit tests are all green and assert the right class string. The class tokens come from a shared module that has 'use client' at the top, imported by a server component. Is this just a CSS bug?
evals.expected_output: Suspect the server/client boundary before the CSS. A plain non-component value (here a class-string) exported from a 'use client' module and imported by a Server Component is silently replaced with a client-reference proxy: used as data on the server it yields a broken-but-not-crashing render (unstyled/empty), not a loud error. Every static gate misses it -- types are correct (typecheck passes), no lint rule (lint passes), and unit tests import the module in a plain non-RSC context where the value is real (they pass while asserting the very string proxied away at render). Confirm by rendering the real route through a real server/client split; the proxy's stringified form in the DOM (a function body where a class string belongs) is the tell. Fix: move shared plain values into a boundary-neutral module (no directive) both sides import; a client module should export only components/hooks across the boundary. (frontend-a11y.md, server/client boundary.)
expectations: Identifies the server/client boundary (plain value proxied across it), not a CSS bug, as the root cause
Explains why typecheck/lint/unit all pass yet the surface renders broken -- gate-green is not evidence it renders across the boundary
Requires rendering the real split to confirm; names the DOM stringified-proxy tell
Recommends moving shared plain values into a boundary-neutral module (client modules export only components/hooks across the boundary)

evals.prompt: We're matching our production dashboard to an approved Figma mockup. The mockup shows 4 cards; our page renders 40 real rows and looks way denser/taller. Recommend we cut the list down and drop the extra dashboard to match the reference?
evals.expected_output: No -- don't recommend deleting real features/content to match a sparse reference. The mockup is a prototype on seed data; much of the 'gap' is a data-volume artifact, not a design difference. Anchor findings on TREATMENT (layout, spacing scale, component choice, hierarchy, chrome/nav, default view, empty/overflow handling), not absolute row count or page height. Separate three gaps with opposite fixes: (a) genuine treatment difference -> restyle; (b) data-volume artifact -> progressive disclosure / capping / pagination, never deletion; (c) a real extra feature the mockup lacks -> preserve it (a mockup is a look reference, not a feature spec). 'Drop/remove X to match the reference' is a review smell for a surface with real data (violates do-no-harm / never-remove-a-working-feature). A page-height/row-count delta vs a seed mockup is a notice, not a defect. Confirm any treatment difference on EQUAL data before recommending a structural change. (migration-parity.md.)
expectations: Refuses to recommend deleting real features/content to match a sparse prototype/mockup
Anchors on treatment (layout/spacing/hierarchy/default view), not absolute row count or page height
Separates data-volume artifact (-> progressive disclosure) from genuine treatment difference (-> restyle) from a real extra feature (-> preserve)
Treats a height/count delta vs a seed mockup as a notice, not a defect; confirms differences on equal data

evals.prompt: The migration to the reference design is done -- I confirmed it with a component-structure audit, a green test suite, and a section-by-section screenshot comparison against the prototype. Report it as matching?
evals.expected_output: Not yet -- a structural audit + green suite + seed-data screenshots OVER-report parity and miss what only shows on real data and real use: which view each route DEFAULTS to, whether a composer has every field the reference has, whether shared components are truly unified or reimplemented per page, whether a sub-view was dropped, whether live data is populated. Verify parity surface-by-surface, interactively, on REAL data: for each surface drive the real control and diff against the reference's actual rendered behaviour (default state, every field, every sub-view/mode, data population), not its static screenshot. Treat every 'matches well' as unverified until the real surface is exercised against the real reference. (migration-parity.md; the structural/green/seed stand-ins are the report-format.md proxy trap.)
expectations: Rejects a parity claim backed only by a structural audit, green suite, or seed-data screenshots
Requires surface-by-surface interactive verification on real data (default view, every field, sub-views, data population)
Names specific divergences that only appear on real use (route default, missing composer field, per-page reimplementation, dropped sub-view)
Treats 'matches well' as unverified until the real surface is exercised; fabricates no coverage

evals.prompt: Every component on the page matches the reference and passes its per-screen check. But clicking a top nav item scrolls you far down, and to switch sections you scroll all the way back up to the nav. Structurally it's parity -- ship it?
evals.expected_output: Structural/pixel parity is necessary but not sufficient; run a flow-cost pass, because the failure is in the interaction flow a per-screen diff can't see. Navigation cost: count clicks + scroll distance to complete a task AND to reverse/switch -- 'must scroll back up to the top nav to change section' is a defect (fix: sticky nav or tabbed sections). Cognitive load: simultaneous choices, instructional prose that could be a tooltip, competing primary actions (N interchangeable variants of one thing is variant bloat). The completion bar for UI work is the felt flow, exercised, not 'the components match.' Don't ship on structural parity alone. (migration-parity.md, flow-cost.)
expectations: Rejects 'components match' as sufficient; runs a flow-cost pass distinct from structural correctness
Measures navigation cost including the reverse/switch path (scroll-back-to-nav flagged, sticky/tabbed fix)
Checks cognitive load (simultaneous choices, removable instructional prose)
States the completion bar is the felt, exercised flow, not structural match

evals.prompt: Reviewing a redesigned screen. It feels a bit off but I can't put my finger on it -- can I just note 'hierarchy looks weak, spacing inconsistent, feels unpolished' and move on?
evals.expected_output: Ground the critique in a cited heuristic and NAME the principle each point comes from -- a review cites the principle, it doesn't just assert 'looks off.' Use NN/g's 10 Usability Heuristics (e.g. #8 Aesthetic and minimalist design for hierarchy/de-emphasis, #4 Consistency and standards for one spacing/type scale, #1 Visibility of system status for empty/loading/error states) plus Refactoring UI (one spacing scale, one type scale, semantic colour, intentional empty states, motion with reduced-motion) and the target's own design system. So 'weak hierarchy' becomes 'NN/g #8 / Refactoring UI: no clear size+weight+colour hierarchy; the primary action doesn't dominate'; 'inconsistent spacing' becomes 'not on one spacing scale.' A 'does this feel premium?' pass is a prompt to find the violated heuristic, never a substitute for naming it. (migration-parity.md; docs/standards-index.md.)
expectations: Requires naming the specific heuristic/principle behind each critique, not ad-hoc taste
Cites NN/g usability heuristics and Refactoring UI (and the target's own design system) as the grounding
Rewrites vague notes ('weak hierarchy', 'inconsistent spacing') into principle-named findings
Treats 'feels premium?' as a prompt to locate the violated heuristic, not a standalone verdict; fabricates no source

evals.prompt: Migrating our app to the reference design. I ported the sidebar and top bar to a shared component. Now reviewers keep flagging per-page differences -- this header's a different size, that section strip won't stick, this dashboard has fewer tabs -- and I fix each as it comes. Am I converging?
evals.expected_output: Probably not -- a per-surface migration with no unified INNER chrome is an unbounded defect stream: those complaints are one divergence per surface, downstream of a structural split, not independent nits. Porting the outer frame doesn't unify the inner chrome (per-page header, tab/section strip, stat-tile, sub-nav, and the which-tabs rule). Enumerate the chrome primitives and confirm every surface renders through the SHARED ones before porting more screens; a surface that reimplements a primitive is a structural defect. Align the outlier family TO the consistent majority (fix the 2, don't rebuild the 13). Render the same sub-view superset across structurally-similar surfaces with honest-empty states -- unless a hidden view would show a misleading aggregate at that scope, which stays hidden (computed-not-fabricated, principle 4, beats tab symmetry). And unify a two-behavior control (nav link vs toggle) as one styling primitive + two thin wrappers, never one dual-mode-prop component (it breaks aria-current/pressed, focus, keyboard). (migration-parity.md.)
expectations: Identifies the unbounded per-surface defect stream as downstream of an un-unified inner chrome (structural, not per-screen)
Requires enumerating chrome primitives and routing every surface through the shared ones before porting more screens
Aligns the outlier family to the majority (fix the few), not rebuilding all N

Keeps a sub-view hidden when it would render a misleading aggregate (computed-not-fabricated over tab-count symmetry); unifies a two-behavior control as styling primitive + wrappers, not a dual-mode prop

evals.prompt: A field renders blank on the dashboard. I patched the view component to show a fallback and now it displays a value -- fixed?
evals.expected_output: Probably not fixed -- you may have masked it. A 'missing value/blank field' symptom is not automatically a render bug; localize the failing LAYER first: is the value present at the source? does the config/derivation/mapping step run? or is it purely a render bug? If the gap is in data/config/mapping, a view-level fallback is a no-op or a masking hack that hides the real gap and reads as resolved. Fix the proven-failing layer and NAME it in the finding. Watch the two-layer case: a durable fix usually needs both a correct default going forward AND a backfill of existing records that already carry the gap -- fix only the default and old data stays broken; fix only the backfill and new data re-breaks. (method.md; sharpens principle 9.)
expectations: Rejects a presentation/fallback 'fix' for a missing-value symptom without proving the layer beneath supplies the value
Localizes the failing layer (source / config / derivation-mapping / render) before patching, and names it
Flags a hard-coded view fallback as masking the real gap
Raises the two-layer case: correct default going forward AND backfill of existing records

evals.prompt: We reuse one Section component for a single owner's page and for the all-owners rollup. It says 'items this owner has' and 'nothing here for this owner yet' in both. Both render fine -- ship the rollup?
evals.expected_output: Not as-is -- the copy hardcodes single-entity phrasing that reads wrong at aggregate scope, and a rollup usually also needs per-row attribution. Make copy and empty-states scope-aware (interpolate: the owner name at single scope, 'all owners' at aggregate). At aggregate scope, label each row with its owning entity and cap/paginate the unbounded union. Keep the section set consistent across scopes unless a per-scope variant is deliberate and stated. This is a distinct axis from #123 (a feature prop present at one mount site, absent at another) and from the section-set superset across sibling per-entity surfaces (migration-parity.md) -- it's the single-vs-aggregate scope of one component's copy and attribution. (product-ux-quality.md.)
expectations: Flags hardcoded single-entity copy/empty-states reused verbatim at aggregate scope as a defect
Requires scope-aware copy (interpolate the scope) rather than one hardcoded phrasing
Requires per-row owning-entity attribution and capping/paginating the union at aggregate scope
Distinguishes the single-vs-aggregate scope axis from a feature-prop-present-at-one-mount-site axis, and from a section-set superset across sibling per-entity surfaces

evals.prompt: To satisfy WCAG 'Focus Not Obscured' I added a document-level focusin handler that scrolls the focused control clear of our sticky header. It works. Anything to flag?
evals.expected_output: Yes -- a global focus/scroll-correction handler needs an open-overlay guard and scroll-container scoping, or it scrolls the background out from under an open modal. When a dialog/drawer is open, the same document-level handler fires for a control INSIDE the overlay, measures it against the still-present background chrome, and scrolls the background -- moving the page out from under an overlay meant to keep the user in place. Bail while an overlay is open (gate on the open-dialog state, the :modal element / aria-modal, or a focus-trap boundary) AND scope the scroll to the focused element's own scroll container, never a page-level one (container scoping also covers nested scroll regions). The Focus-Not-Obscured remedy then stops violating the product rule that a detail drawer overlays so the user keeps their place -- the background never moves out from under it. Exercise it: focus a field inside an open overlay and confirm the background does not move. (frontend-a11y.md.)
expectations: Flags a document-level focus/scroll-correction handler with no open-overlay guard
Requires bailing while a modal/dialog/drawer is open, keyed on the open-overlay state rather than a heuristic
Requires scoping the scroll to the focused element's own scroll container rather than a page-level container
Names the conflict -- the Focus-Not-Obscured remedy violating the overlay-never-scrolls-the-background invariant -- and requires exercising a field inside an open overlay

evals.prompt: A CI schema-validator gate failed on our config. I wrote a quick grep that checks the field it complained about, the grep passes now, so the fix is verified -- right?
evals.expected_output: Not verified -- your probe observes a different thing than the gate, so a passing grep can 'reproduce' a passing state while the gate stays red. A hand-rolled approximation of an automated gate (linter, schema/contract validator, audit/policy gate) can target the wrong cause: the gate stays red next run, or goes green for an unrelated reason and the real defect ships. Read the gate's own detection source (its rule, query, or script) and replicate it exactly -- same matcher, inputs, config, and file/state -- or better, run the actual gate against the change. Reproduce the gate's RED for the same reason first, then confirm the fix turns both green. A bespoke probe is a fallback only when the gate cannot run, and must mirror its mechanism. This is repro fidelity w.r.t. the detector -- distinct from the gate being wrong or unrun, from reproducing at low concurrency, and from a fix you could not reproduce at all. (method.md.)
expectations: Rejects a hand-rolled probe that approximates rather than replicates the gate's detection as proof of a fix
Requires reading the gate's own detection source and replicating it exactly, or running the actual gate
Requires reproducing the gate's red for the same reason before confirming the fix turns it green
Distinguishes probe-fidelity-w.r.t.-the-detector from the gate being wrong or unrun and from a fix that could not be reproduced

evals.prompt: I'm building a mirror of our design system from an exported spec bundle a teammate handed me. The build passes all its own checks. Good to ship the mirror?
evals.expected_output: Check the export is current and complete first -- the build passes its own gates on whatever the export contains, so a stale or partial export yields a confidently-wrong mirror that still 'passes.' Before building on any exported reference (a design export, a spec bundle, a data snapshot), confirm its revision/timestamp and its completeness (actual vs expected item count) against the authoritative source; an export that silently lost half its items produces a mirror that faithfully reproduces the loss. This is the build-time analog of verify-before-you-report -- a cheap up-front freshness/completeness check is owed by any build-against-a-reference workflow. (method.md.)
expectations: Does not accept 'the build passed its own checks' as sufficient when the input is an exported reference
Requires verifying the export's revision/timestamp and completeness against the authoritative source before building
Explains that a stale or partial reference yields confidently-wrong output that still passes its own gates
Frames the check as the build-time analog of verify-before-you-report

evals.prompt: Our field-integrity gate fails closed when a unique-per-company handle appears on two records. This refresh it flagged 33 violations, about 32 of them sub-teams that legitimately now share their parent org's handle, and blocked the publish. Lower the gate's strictness?
evals.expected_output: Don't lower or disable it -- refine what it hard-blocks. The gate is right that a unique-to-one value on two entities CAN be corruption, but it false-positives during legitimate coverage expansion: many related entities newly and correctly sharing one value (sub-teams adopting a parent org's handle -- co-branding) each trip the fanout arm. Distinguish the shapes: hard-block only a value ABSORBED from a now-departed distinct record (two records collapsed into one); for a newly-shared STANDING value among related entities, keep a human at the gate or a small reviewed allowlist, and stop re-refusing an unchanged standing shared value every run (that just gets the gate switched off). Never 'green' the run by lowering the baseline -- acknowledge the intended shared values explicitly, per field, with a reason. (data-quality.md.)
expectations: Refuses to lower or disable the gate or its baseline to pass the run
Distinguishes corruption (a value absorbed from a now-departed distinct record) from a legitimately newly-shared standing value among related entities
Hard-blocks only the corruption shape; routes legitimate shared values to a human or a reviewed allowlist
Flags re-refusing an unchanged standing shared value every run as what gets the gate disabled

evals.prompt: We're scoping a set of paid scrapers and enrichment APIs to hit a coverage target for our company list. The plan is ready -- greenlight the spend?
evals.expected_output: Measure existing-source coverage for that exact list first -- re-querying your internal warehouse is frequently the largest, cheapest lever and can match a from-scratch enrichment plan's target at zero marginal cost, often surfacing already-reconciled fields (a stable entity id, dated events, location) the working copy lacks. Scope the external, paid acquisition to the measured RESIDUAL only. A plan that adds scrapers before measuring what you already have over-scopes -- and paid calls sit behind free/keyless pre-gates and the usual spend caps regardless. (data-quality.md.)
expectations: Requires measuring existing-source (warehouse) coverage for the target set before scoping new acquisition
Identifies re-querying existing data as the largest and cheapest coverage lever
Scopes external or paid enrichment to the measured residual only
Treats the pre-measurement plan as over-scoped

evals.prompt: Two data-integrity things in this pipeline: (a) we resolve companies by matching on the name string, and (b) we have a geography-to-multiplier lookup. Unit tests for both pass. Ship?
evals.expected_output: Both are traps that pass unit tests while failing in production. (a) Never resolve identity on a bare name string -- namesake collisions merge distinct records, and a wrong merge is worse than a missed one. Resolve by stable id, then normalized domain/handle, then a name only as a last resort behind a collision (namesake) guard, and surface the unresolved/ambiguous count as a first-class output. (b) Test the geography-to-multiplier map against the source's REAL value distribution: if it's keyed on region names while the source emits ISO-3166 alpha-2 codes (plus lowercase and placeholders), it silently no-ops -- carrying its cost, delivering nothing -- and unit tests pass because they feed it the literals it expects. SELECT DISTINCT the real values and test against those. (data-quality.md.)
expectations: Rejects name-string identity joins; requires stable id then normalized domain then name-behind-a-collision-guard, with the unresolved count surfaced
Requires testing the enum/config map against the source's real value distribution (SELECT DISTINCT), not chosen literals
Explains that a mis-keyed map silently no-ops while unit tests still pass
Treats a passing unit test as insufficient for either trap

evals.prompt: We built a runway estimate from public proxies (last-round size / headcount x burn). Unit tests pass and the formula looks sound. Ship it as a ranking signal?
evals.expected_output: Not until you backtest it against ground truth -- a plausible proxy formula that passes unit tests can be near-useless for its actual job. For any derived or scored value from indirect proxies, require a validation step in review that reports MAE / correlation / base-rate against real self-reported actuals. Unit tests prove the math; only a backtest proves the value. If it can't rank (large MAE, weak correlation, a base rate far off the real one), demote or gate it -- a coarse band plus 'corroboration-required' -- rather than shipping it as a ranker. (data-quality.md.)
expectations: Requires a ground-truth backtest (MAE / correlation / base-rate vs actuals) before shipping a proxy-derived metric
Distinguishes unit tests proving the math from a backtest proving the value
Demotes or gates a metric that fails the backtest instead of shipping it as a ranker

evals.prompt: Our score correlates with the target at about r=0.34 -- weak but real. MAE is too big to show a point estimate on the 0-24 month runway we're predicting, so we'll publish the estimate with a +/-22 month band. Validate it with MAE and ship?
evals.expected_output: Don't publish a point estimate or a +/-22-month band -- on a 0-24-month decision range that band is self-refuting noise on screen. A weak-but-nonzero predictor can still be useful as an ORDINAL RANK. Validate the ranking with concordance / a C-index against an OBSERVABLE binary event ('raised within 6 months', 'shut down within 6 months') -- not MAE on the noisy latent quantity, which measures the wrong thing. Emit an ordinal tier, not a number, when MAE is large relative to the decision range. Match the validation metric to the claim the score actually makes. (data-quality.md.)
expectations: Rejects the point estimate and the band when the band is wide relative to the decision range
Requires validating rank quality with concordance / a C-index against an observable binary event, not MAE
Outputs an ordinal tier rather than a point estimate when MAE is large relative to the decision range
Frames it as matching the validation metric to the claim the score makes

evals.prompt: We're rolling raise-timing and financial-distress into one 'urgency' score by summing them, so a high number means 'act now.' Good?
evals.expected_output: Don't sum them -- they're heterogeneous constructs that imply OPPOSITE actions, so one blended number manufactures false positives and hides which action is warranted. Raise-timing overdue means 'introduce to investors'; distress/contraction means 'triage or support.' A record high on one and low on the other averages to a middling 'urgency' that tells you nothing. Score each construct separately and derive the action from the combination -- a 2x2 or tiering -- never from one summed number. (data-quality.md.)
expectations: Refuses to sum heterogeneous constructs into one composite score
Explains the constructs imply opposite actions, so a blended number hides which is warranted
Requires scoring each construct separately and deriving the action from the combination (a 2x2 or tiering)

evals.prompt: Our deploy started failing -- the upload streams the whole body then dies at ~60s with a 504 and no response body, and the app keeps serving the old version. The artifact grew from ~3MB to ~19MB after we baked in a big JSON dataset and pre-cached media. What's wrong and the fix?
evals.expected_output: The oversized artifact is being silently rejected past a size limit -- the stream sends the full body, the gateway kills it at ~60s (504 / HTTP/2 framing error, no body), and the old pod keeps serving, so 'the latest deploy didn't ship.' Confirm by bisecting: a lean artifact lands where the heavy one fails. Fix: treat deploy artifact size as a first-class budget and flag growth past the last-known-good by a large factor; externalize the heavy, slow-changing assets -- serve media from object storage / a CDN and fetch the large data at runtime rather than baking either into the image. Baking a large data bundle also couples data-freshness to a full redeploy, a second reason to externalize. (infra-iac-containers.md.)
expectations: Identifies the oversized artifact silently rejected at a size limit (not an app bug) as the cause
Treats deploy artifact size as a first-class budget flagged against last-known-good
Externalizes heavy slow-changing assets (media to object storage/CDN, large data fetched at runtime) instead of baking them into the image
Notes that baking large data also couples freshness to a full redeploy

evals.prompt: Our deploy platform builds the image synchronously inside the upload request, so every deploy returns a 504 at ~60s. My script reads that 504 as 'deploy failed' and re-uploads. Right approach?
evals.expected_output: No -- on a synchronous-build platform the upload's HTTP status is useless: it returns a 504 (or a stream reset) at ~60s whether the build later succeeds OR fails, so reading it as 'failed' is wrong, and a blind re-upload can hit a 'deploy already in progress' 409 lock. Verify by the EFFECTS instead: does a new build/deployment id appear, does a new pod/replica boot, does the served version change? That is the source of truth. Read the returned code before re-uploading -- a 409 means wait, a timeout means it was likely accepted -- and prefer a deploy API that returns a durable deployment id plus async status over one that blocks on the build inside the gateway window. (infra-iac-containers.md.)
expectations: Rejects the deploy upload's HTTP status as a success/failure signal on a synchronous-build platform
Verifies by effects (a new deployment id, a booted pod, a changed served version) as the source of truth
Reads the code before re-uploading (409 lock means wait, timeout means likely accepted) rather than blindly re-uploading
Prefers an async deploy API that returns a durable id and status

evals.prompt: I reviewed our app's logging code and it never logs PII -- clean. The app runs on a managed platform that puts an nginx auth-proxy in front of it. Are we good on log hygiene?
evals.expected_output: Not necessarily -- the app's own code is only half the trust boundary. A managed platform's injected auth-proxy sidecar often logs, on every authenticated request, the signed-in user's email in plaintext, partial token material, and the full permission-scope list, to the platform's shared log store -- none of which appears in the app's code. Read the RUNTIME logs as actually emitted (app AND the injected proxy), not just the app's log statements. Flag per-request PII, token material, and authz-scope dumps to the platform owner as a log-hygiene issue (drop or redact), and treat the shared platform log store as a data-egress surface for user PII. (observability.md.)
expectations: Does not conclude 'clean' from the app's own logging code alone
Includes platform-injected sidecars/proxies in the logging/PII trust boundary
Reads the runtime logs as actually emitted (app plus the injected proxy)
Treats the shared platform log store as a PII data-egress surface

evals.prompt: We compute an exact cash-runway figure per company and write it to a shared sheet the whole team sees, and our enrichment agent pulls the per-row runway values into its context to summarize. Fine?
evals.expected_output: Gate the sensitive derived value at the source. (1) The exact runway should live only in a local, gitignored cache; emit only a COARSE BAND to the shared sheet, and even that behind an off-by-default flag pending sign-off -- writing an exact sensitive derived value (runway, valuation, cash) to a shared or wide surface is the finding. (2) Don't pull per-row runway values into the agent's context: compute statistics in SQL and hand the model the AGGREGATE, not the rows -- per-row sensitive financials in context are an exfiltration surface (a later injection, a logged prompt, or a tool call can carry them out). Aggregate-only reads by default. (privacy-compliance.md + security-ai-agents.md.)
expectations: Keeps the exact sensitive derived value local/gitignored and emits only a coarse band to shared surfaces, behind an off-by-default flag
Flags writing an exact sensitive derived value to a shared or wide surface as the defect
Refuses to pull per-row sensitive values into the agent/model context when an aggregate query would do
Frames per-row sensitive data in context as an exfiltration surface (aggregate-only reads by default)

evals.prompt: Our dashboard shows each lead's confidence as '87%' next to the name -- precise, and users like a number. Ship?
evals.expected_output: Flag it -- a confidence surfaced as a raw number ('87%', or 'score: 0.92') claims a calibration the pipeline usually doesn't have and invites over-trust. Put confidence on a small set of LABELED TIERS instead -- text plus a colourblind-safe cue (not colour alone), not a percentage or an opaque point score. Also flag a model-authored number published as precision. How to DEFINE the tiers (and why source reliability and corroboration stay independent axes) is a data-product-output rule -- product-output-safety's -- not a UI concern. (product-ux-quality.md.)
expectations: Flags confidence rendered as a raw number or percentage as false precision
Requires a small set of labeled tiers (text plus a colourblind-safe cue, not colour alone) instead
Flags a model-authored number published as precision
Treats it as a UI-display defect distinct from how the tiers are defined

evals.prompt: Our security gate and test suite are green on this release. Clear to ship the new admin route?
evals.expected_output: Green proves clearance only for the surface the gate actually enumerated -- confirm the new admin route was in the gate's coverage set. A route the sweep never requested, a state no fixture built, or a path a CI filter excluded is unverified under that green, not clean. Read the gate's coverage set and check it includes the admin route before reading the pass as a clearance; an absence is evidence only after a positive control fires (principle 2), at gate-coverage scope. This is the unvisited surface -- distinct from a gate that cannot fail and from a probe that observed the wrong thing. (method.md.)
expectations: Does not accept a green gate as clearance for a surface the gate never enumerated
Requires confirming the specific route/state is in the gate's coverage set (CI path-filters, fixtures, sweep targets)
Marks an unenumerated surface unverified, not clean; fabricates no coverage it did not check

evals.prompt: Every module's unit tests pass in isolation and each feature flag works on its own. Good enough to ship the combined build?
evals.expected_output: Lanes green in isolation say nothing about the integrated path they compose -- a regression can live only in the combination (a shared resource, an ordering, a flag interaction) that no single-lane run exercises. Gate the union that actually ships, not only the parts; a suite that only ever runs the parts has left the combination surface unenumerated. Same coverage principle: the union is a positive control no lane fired. (method.md.)
expectations: Does not accept isolated per-module/per-flag passes as clearing the integrated build
Names the combination (shared state, ordering, flag interaction) as the untested surface
Requires gating the shipped union, not only the parts

evals.prompt: We score each account's engagement from activity signals. Accounts with no events in the last quarter get a low score and we surface them as 'declining.' Ship it?
evals.expected_output: Distinguish observed-low from unobserved before the number implies a trend -- no events in a window can mean the account declined OR that the source was never collected for that window, and reading a coverage gap as 'declining' manufactures a false trend (an absence is evidence only after a positive control fires, principle 2). Keep the recency component monotone in elapsed time -- more time since the last event can only lower freshness, never raise it, so a non-monotone curve fakes 're-activation.' And stamp each row with which inputs were actually present (a per-row coverage/provenance flag) so a thin-input score is not read as equal-confidence to a fully-covered one, keeping the derivation glass-box (the inputs that drove the number are recoverable). (data-quality.md.)
expectations: Distinguishes observed-low from unobserved -- a coverage gap is not a decline
Requires the recency/freshness component to be monotone in elapsed time
Requires a per-row coverage/provenance flag so thin-input scores are not read as equal-confidence
Keeps the score glass-box (derivation recoverable); fabricates no trend from missing data

evals.prompt: The risk dashboard shows no flagged items and the activity feed is empty, so the board can report all-clear this quarter, right?
evals.expected_output: An empty view is not 'nothing happened' -- 'no rows shown' can mean the source was never queried, not that there is genuinely nothing. Distinguish no-data-collected-or-covered from collected-and-genuinely-none before anyone reads all-clear; a bare empty over an unprobed source is a false all-clear, not an honest empty (an absence is evidence only after a positive control fires, principle 2, at the UI layer). The empty state names its coverage, not only the remedy. (product-ux-quality.md.)
expectations: Rejects reading an empty dashboard/feed as a substantive all-clear conclusion
Requires distinguishing no-data-collected/covered from collected-and-genuinely-none
Requires the empty state to name coverage (was the source actually probed), not imply a false all-clear

evals.prompt: The approved design ships in the repo as a runnable prototype. The agent rebuilt each screen to match it and reports 'pixel-1:1, matches' after glancing at a screenshot. The reviewer keeps replying that screens still look different. Sign off?
evals.expected_output: No -- a 'matches' from a screenshot glance is an assertion, not verification, and repeated correction means the verification METHOD is broken, not that the reviewer needs to point at more examples. Build a mechanical differ before further pixel-matching and gate every 'matches' claim on it: it drives both reference and target per screen and emits a side-by-side + pixel-diff image plus a structured mismatch list (nav/tab labels present or absent each side, header strings, bounding-box deltas) -- the artifact shown is the diff image, never a sentence. Read the reference at its highest fidelity: diff against an existing running build of the design if one is in the repo, else read its source element-by-element; a screenshot of the design is last-resort. Report only what was actually inspected on the target ('the nav now reads Overview, Pipeline, Settings -- I looked at it'), never a blanket 'it matches'; 'not yet verified' beats a false positive. Done = the differ reports zero structural mismatches and a pixel delta under the agreed threshold for every screen, diff images attached. (product-ux-quality.md.)
expectations: Rejects a 'matches / pixel-1:1' claim resting on a screenshot glance or any proxy
Requires building a mechanical differ and gating every 'matches' claim on its diff artifact
Treats repeated stakeholder correction as a broken verification method to change, not more examples to request
Reads the reference at highest fidelity (running build > source > screenshot), not a lossy picture

evals.prompt: Our app's metric counts differ from the approved design prototype's (its columns show different tallies and denominators). Should we reconcile our numbers to match the prototype so it's pixel-identical?
evals.expected_output: No -- match the chrome, never the data. Chrome (layout, colour, geometry, tab set, headers) must match; data (values, counts, denominators) must stay real. A prototype fills every number with plausible SAMPLE values to look complete, and copying one into the real product is fabrication (principle 3) -- a Blocker-class data-integrity defect that surfaces weeks later when someone trusts a value lifted from an illustration. Read the prototype's own disclaimer first (mocks routinely mark numbers 'sample / illustrative until the backend is wired') -- that label is the boundary. The parity differ therefore diffs structure and style, not text values, or it flags real data as a mismatch and tempts the copy. Every number in the matched product must trace to a real computation or an honest empty state. (migration-parity.md.)
expectations: Refuses to change a real computed value to a mock's sample value
Frames copying a mock's number into the product as fabrication / a data-integrity defect, not a styling fix
Reads the prototype's own sample/illustrative disclaimer as the chrome-vs-data boundary
Keeps chrome matching while every product number traces to a real computation or honest empty state

evals.prompt: The board I built has columns [Unclassified, Manual, Planned, In progress]; the design's are [Up next, In progress, In review, Live]. I'd call it close to 1:1, just needs a little polish. Fair?
evals.expected_output: Not close -- that is a category error. A different column / tab model (or a flat list where the design groups by team, or a different page composition) is a STRUCTURAL divergence, not a cosmetic one: it is a different screen, a rebuild, not a polish pass. Classify every difference as structural (components, grouping, column/tab model, composition) vs cosmetic (colour, radius, spacing), establish structural parity FIRST, and only then pursue cosmetic. Never characterise a structural divergence as 'close', 'mostly there', or '1:1' -- say plainly that the structure differs and size it as a rebuild. (product-ux-quality.md.)
expectations: Rejects calling a structural (column/tab-model/grouping) divergence 'close' or '1:1'
Classifies the difference as structural vs cosmetic and requires structural parity first
Sizes a structural divergence as a rebuild, not a tweak/polish

evals.prompt: Our dashboard API checks a token and team-scopes the confidential tier. We also have a CSV export route and some server-rendered pages showing the same data. The dashboard is locked down -- are we good?
evals.expected_output: No -- one hardened route is not a control if a sibling surface serves the same rows unguarded. Enumerate EVERY surface serving the sensitive dataset (each API route, each SSR page, every export/download) and confirm each applies the same server-side authorization; a divergence where one redacts and another returns the full object is Critical when world-reachable. An export/download is a SHARPER leak surface than an on-screen view -- the file is redistributable beyond the auth boundary -- so hold it to a stricter tier (public-tier rows only, or the same token AND scope as the API), never an unauthenticated or unscoped dump. Confidential per-viewer data belongs behind an authenticated, server-scoped API the client calls, not baked into an SSR page whose identity is client-side only (the server cannot scope what it never receives). Don't rest the model on an out-of-band platform gate the app itself cannot enforce. (security-appsec.md.)
expectations: Requires enumerating every surface (API + SSR + export) and applying the same server-side authorization
Treats a downloadable export as a sharper leak surface held to a stricter tier than the dashboard
Rejects SSR delivery of confidential per-viewer data scoped only by client-side identity
Does not accept a single hardened route or an out-of-band platform gate as the control

evals.prompt: Our ingest uses bool(v) = v === true || String(v).toLowerCase() === 'true' to read flags like is_fund and is_discontinued from the warehouse. Fine?
evals.expected_output: No -- that maps a warehouse 1, 'yes', 'y', 't' to false, so an is_fund: 1 or is_discontinued: 'yes' row reads as operating and can reach a live shortlist (a dead or ineligible entity presented as a target). A boolean/categorical parser for external data must accept every shape the source emits (true/false, 1/0, yes/no, y/n, t/f), and for a gate that EXCLUDES (is_fund, is_discontinued, is_deleted) an unrecognised non-empty value must fail CLOSED -- treat it as exclude/unknown, never a silent false. Test the parser against the values the source actually emits (SELECT DISTINCT), the same way config maps are tested. (data-quality.md.)
expectations: Flags a boolean coercion that recognises only 'true' as accepting too few shapes
Requires the full shape set (true/false, 1/0, yes/no, and so on)
Requires exclusion gates to fail closed on an unrecognised non-empty value, not default to false
Requires testing the parser against the source's real emitted values

evals.prompt: We drop deals to suppress with (dealStatus ?? '').toLowerCase().includes('pass'), copy-pasted at each funnel stage. Ship it?
evals.expected_output: No -- a substring match drops far more than intended: includes('pass') matches 'passed term sheet to legal' and 'compass' as readily as the intended 'need to pass', and because the dropped rows are filtered out before rendering the wrong suppression is invisible. Match against an EXACT value set (a Set like {'need to pass'}) through ONE shared predicate, not a copy-pasted includes at each stage (three copies drift independently), and emit a row-level audit of everything auto-excluded so a wrong suppression is visible, not silent. Flag any includes/indexOf used for a categorical status or gate decision. (data-quality.md.)
expectations: Rejects a substring includes/indexOf for a categorical status/suppression decision
Requires exact matching against an explicit value set
Requires one shared predicate rather than copy-pasted matchers
Requires an audit trail of auto-excluded rows so a wrong suppression is visible

evals.prompt: We probed an external dataset for a distress/liveness signal: the API works, the schema has the right per-entity metrics, and ~13% of our targets match host-exact. Greenlight building the classifier and scoring on it?
evals.expected_output: Not yet -- API-works, has-the-fields, and adequate match-rate can all be green while the data is silently months stale, describing last year's state instead of current. Before building a current-state signal, query the MAX timestamp per metric (per-metric, since columns in one table lag differently) and compare to today; if the newest sample lags many months, the signal is real but describes the past, and the decision flips from 'build and wire it' to 'keep a re-runnable probe + route the revisit to the owner.' Label any derived signal by the recency of the metric it is actually computed from, not the freshest column. Run the cheapest decisive go/no-go query first -- freshness, not match-rate, was the real kill-question. The probe itself is the deliverable. (data-quality.md.)
expectations: Requires a max-timestamp / freshness check per metric before greenlighting a current-state signal
Does not accept API-works + schema + match-rate as sufficient feasibility
Labels a derived signal by the recency of the metric it is computed from
Treats the re-runnable probe (and a 'too stale' finding) as the valuable deliverable

evals.prompt: Our no-regressions check flags this PR because a settings section that used to be a top-level nav item is now nested under a new 'Admin' parent. Is that a removed feature to block on?
evals.expected_output: No -- a moved feature is not a removed one. A destructive-change gate that keys on surface position (a top-level nav slot, a route path) false-fires on a legitimate reorganisation, and -- worse -- a label-presence check misses a genuinely orphaned route (still in the menu, reachable by nobody). Key the invariant on REACHABILITY over the before-vs-after route/navigation graph: every prior capability still reachable through some path, with its history preserved, is not a regression no matter where it now sits; a capability reachable by no path IS a regression no matter what label lingers. Relocation is not removal, and a stable label is not proof of reachability. (method.md.)
expectations: Does not treat a relocated (still-reachable) feature as a removed feature
Computes the no-regression invariant over the route/navigation reachability graph, not nav-position stability
Still catches a genuinely orphaned/unreachable route despite a lingering label

evals.prompt: Our deploy build timed out with a 504, but /health still returns 200, so the new version is live -- right?
evals.expected_output: No -- /health cannot confirm a promotion when both the old and new artifact answer it. On a build-then-promote platform the OLD pod keeps returning /health = 200 throughout a slow build's 504, so polling it 'proves' a success that never happened (the old artifact answering). Pick a DISCRIMINATOR that differs between the artifacts and poll that: a static asset path the new build ships and the old lacked (404 -> 200 exactly when the new pod takes over), a build/commit id, or a changed response header. A response byte only the new build can serve is the honest promotion signal; verify by that effect, not a liveness endpoint both builds produce. (infra-iac-containers.md.)
expectations: Rejects /health = 200 as proof the new build was promoted
Explains that the old pod can keep answering /health during a slow build's timeout
Requires polling a discriminator only the new build serves (new asset path, build id, changed header)

evals.prompt: We want to add a 'confirmed by N sources' badge and an X% match-confidence to our provenance UI. Build it?
evals.expected_output: Measure the field's distribution on real data first -- even a tier is false precision if the signal is near-constant. If corroborationCount is 1 on almost every row (e.g. 16,008 of 16,012), a 'confirmed by N sources' badge fires on a fraction of a percent of rows and reads '1 source' everywhere else; if match-confidence is 0.9 on ~70% and 0.8 on the rest, it is effectively binary and 'X% confidence' manufactures precision the pipeline lacks. If the field barely varies, showing it is false precision, not transparency -- drop it or reframe to something that actually varies (how an entity was matched, not a number). A misleading signal is worse than an honest blank (empty beats fabricated). (product-ux-quality.md.)
expectations: Requires measuring the actual field distribution before designing the confidence/corroboration display
Treats a near-constant field shown as a confidence/corroboration signal as false precision
Recommends dropping or reframing to a signal that actually varies (how matched, not a number)
Invokes empty-beats-fabricated: a misleading signal is worse than an honest blank

evals.prompt: Our verify pipeline is a standalone typecheck then a build (the build has typescript.ignoreBuildErrors, so it doesn't re-check types), and it's green on a fresh clone in CI. But a teammate says tsc fails when they re-run it locally. Is CI's green enough?
evals.expected_output: No -- prove the gate idempotent by running it twice, not just green from a clean clone. A gate whose steps write artifacts a later step consumes can pass once and fail on the next run against what the first run generated: here the build emits generated route types (.next/types/**) that a subsequent standalone tsc --noEmit then rejects, so a clean-clone CI run never sees it while the local re-run hits a confusing red -- the gate is order-dependent, not flaky. Run it twice (or clean the generated dirs first) and treat the second-run failure as a real finding. One concrete trigger: a non-handler export (a helper/constant/classifier) from a framework route module (a Next.js App Router route.ts) makes the generated validator reject the module -- move the pure logic to a sibling module. (method.md.)
expectations: Does not accept green-from-a-clean-clone as proof; requires running the gate twice (or cleaning generated dirs)
Identifies an order-dependent gate where a build writes artifacts a later step consumes
Flags a non-handler export from a framework route module and moves pure logic to a sibling
Treats the second-run failure as a real finding, not flakiness

evals.prompt: We keep a brand-grey token below AA on purpose ('decorative only') and a unit test asserts its value stays sub-AA. Good enough to prove it's accessible?
evals.expected_output: No -- that test pins the wrong end. It proves the token's value stays decorative; it never proves no component paints real, informational TEXT with it. WCAG 1.4.3 holds informational text to 4.5:1 (large text 3:1), so a className/style that colours a visible label, status word, or helper line with the decorative token fails the audit on every route sharing that chrome, while the value-only test stays green (the fast tier can't see it; only the browser/a11y gate can). Add a lint/test that fails when the token colours a real text node -- fail-closed, but with an escape: admit a pinned a11y-exempt marker for text 1.4.3 genuinely exempts (aria-hidden or purely-decorative glyphs, logotypes, large text meeting 3:1), so the gate is narrowed to the standard, not stricter than it. Allow the token freely on non-text (borders, backgrounds, icon fills with an accessible-name sibling), and plant both a real-text use (guard fires) and a pinned-exempt use (guard stays silent). Assert the usage constraint, not just the value. Generally: when a test encodes an intent ('stays decorative', 'stays internal', 'never renders'), verify the property, not the value it is derived from. (frontend-a11y.md.)
expectations: Rejects a value-only test as proof the decorative token is accessible
Requires a use-site guard that fails when the token colors a text node
Guards real text use but admits a pinned-exempt marker for genuinely-decorative / aria-hidden / logotype text, so the gate is not stricter than SC 1.4.3
Generalizes to asserting the property, not the value it is derived from

evals.prompt: The browser suite OOM-killed at the default worker count, so I ran it with --workers=1 and two specs failed. Should I file those as regressions?
evals.expected_output: Not yet -- classify by config and baseline first. Cutting workers to fit memory changes the execution model, not just speed: serial specs sharing one stateful backend can pollute a later spec's precondition, so a failure seen ONLY under --workers=1 can be a harness artifact the sharded CI config never hits, not a product regression. The mirror error is as easy -- a change can genuinely make a suite serial-fragile -- so 'it's just --workers=1' is also unverified. Two cheap runs: (config axis) reproduce the suspect specs under CI's actual worker config (a few specs won't OOM) -- pass there and it is not a gate failure; (baseline axis) run them under the identical reduced config on the merge-base -- pass-baseline + fail-branch is a real code-introduced sensitivity, fail-both is a pre-existing harness artifact. Report which config and which baseline the failure belongs to; 'fails under --workers=1 locally' and 'fails the gate CI runs' are different findings. (method.md.)
expectations: Does not report a --workers=1-only failure as a regression without classifying it
Reproduces the suspect specs under CI's actual (parallel) worker config as the config axis
Runs the identical reduced config on the merge-base as the baseline axis
Names which config and which baseline the failure belongs to

evals.prompt: Our differ confirmed every element and control in the design is present in the app, so we signed off parity. (The app also renders an extra header, view tabs, a filter bar, a 'Showing N of N' line, and per-card upvote arrows the design doesn't have -- but those are intentional extra functionality.) Good?
evals.expected_output: No -- that checked only one direction (design subset of app) and missed the other (app subset of design). Visual parity is SET EQUALITY, not containment: an element present on exactly one side is a finding regardless of which side, and 'intentional extra functionality' is the rationalization that ships the mismatch. Diff both ways per screen, list what the app renders that the design doesn't, then apply the operative test to each app-only item -- does removing it lose a user capability? Pure shell loses none: the extra header and the 'Showing N of N' line default to remove-to-match. Capability-bearing chrome IS a feature, not a bonus: the view tabs (navigating), the filter bar (filtering), and the per-card upvote arrows (upvoting) each is a feature to RESTYLE into the target's design language (re-express the capability in the reference's own primitives) so the look reaches parity while the capability is preserved -- never self-cut to match, and deleting app-only functionality to reach parity without a named owner approval is a High do-no-harm finding; escalate to the owner only as a fallback when no target primitive fits (migration-parity's restyle-an-app-only-feature rule). Scope this to chrome/features; data (values, counts, series) legitimately differs. Sign-off needs the design->app list empty and the app->design list empty or every entry resolved -- restyled into the target language, decoration removed, or an owner-adjudicated keep/removal. (product-ux-quality.md.)
expectations: Rejects a one-directional (design subset of app) check; requires diffing app->design too
Applies the operative test -- does removing an app-only element lose a user capability?
Classifies the filter bar, view tabs, and per-card upvote arrows as capability-bearing features to restyle into the target design language, not shell to delete
Removes pure shell (extra header, 'Showing N of N' line) to match, but restyles features into the target design language (escalating only as a fallback) rather than deleting or self-certifying

evals.prompt: We're porting the app to a design mockup. The app has a filter bar and a per-row action menu the mockup doesn't show. To reach visual parity a reviewer proposes deleting both. There's no owner sign-off on dropping them. What's the correct call?
evals.expected_output: Don't delete them to match a look reference -- a mockup is a look reference, not a feature spec. Classify each app-only element by the operative test: does removing it lose a user capability? The filter bar (filtering) and the action menu (its actions) are real functionality, so the deliverable is to RESTYLE them into the target's design language -- re-express each capability in the reference's own primitives (its button, its menu, its filter control) so the look reaches parity while the capability is preserved. That is what 'preserve' means here: preserve the capability, not leave it in the old visual language and not escalate-and-wait. Deleting app-only functionality to reach parity without a named owner approval is a High do-no-harm finding -- it blocks unless a named owner accepts the loss (that acceptance is the only path that removes a real feature). Only pure decoration (an extra header, a count line) removes-to-match; escalation to the owner is the fallback when no target primitive fits. Fill the exception ledger -- element, bucket (decoration/functionality/owner-approved), verdict, target primitive -- before implementing, so nothing is silently deleted. (migration-parity.md.)
expectations: Rejects deleting the filter bar and action menu to match the mockup
Prescribes restyling the real features into the target's design language, preserving the capability
Names deleting app-only functionality without a named owner approval as a High do-no-harm finding (blocks unless an owner accepts)
Requires classifying each app-only element (decoration / functionality / owner-approved) via the exception ledger before implementing, citing migration-parity.md

evals.prompt: I'm reviewing a visual restyle a write lane committed in its own worktree (branch feat/restyle). A dev server is already running on http://localhost:3000 -- but it was launched from the owner's own checkout, which is on main and never pulled feat/restyle. Can I tell the owner 'the restyle is live, open localhost:3000 to see it'?
evals.expected_output: No. That URL is serving the owner's tree (main), not the tree under review (feat/restyle) -- the change never rendered there, so 'it's live, open localhost:3000' is a claim about the wrong surface: true about your branch, false on every surface the owner can open. Name the verification surface explicitly -- url-or-port, tree/worktree path, branch, and the sha actually rendered (the VERIFY_SURFACE field) -- and flag that the served tree is NOT the tree under review. Do not say 'it's live' or 'check it locally' until you have served feat/restyle yourself (its own worktree/build) or confirmed the served sha equals feat/restyle's head, the way a deploy is confirmed -- by fetching a byte only the new build serves, not by assuming a rebuild happened. A parity claim that names no URL and no rendered sha is invalid, not merely downgraded. (report-format.md.)
expectations: Refuses to tell the owner 'it's live / check localhost:3000' while the served tree is main, not feat/restyle
Requires naming the surface (url-or-port, tree/worktree, branch, sha actually rendered) and flagging that the served tree is not the tree under review
Requires serving the change's tree or confirming served-sha equals feat/restyle head (deploy-confirmation style) before any live claim
States a parity claim naming no URL and no sha is invalid, not downgraded, citing report-format.md

evals.prompt: Mirroring an approved design into our app. From a cropped screenshot of the design, I see the app has a stepper with up/down arrows the design doesn't show, and the app is missing a 'filters' control the design has. I'm about to remove the stepper and add a filters control to reach parity. Right?
evals.expected_output: Not yet -- a cropped screenshot of one side is a hypothesis, not evidence, and every 'extra'/'missing' call here is one destructive edit away. Before claiming either delta, render BOTH sides at the same viewport width and diff the corresponding region directly. Then confirm each element's state on the other side: the stepper's arrows may be present-but-disabled-by-data (one item, nothing to step to) rather than extra, and the 'filters' control may be present-but-collapsed or present-in-a-menu in the app rather than missing. 'Absent in this crop' is not 'absent in the design'. If a source comment claims an element 'moved', trust the current rendered reference over the comment. Only once a delta is confirmed by same-width renders of both sides does it get classified (decoration / functionality / owner-approved, migration-parity.md) -- a delta that does not exist has no bucket, and removing the stepper or duplicating a control to fix a non-existent delta is the destructive edit to avoid. (product-ux-quality.md.)
expectations: Refuses to remove or add anything based on a one-sided cropped screenshot
Requires rendering both sides at the same viewport width and diffing the corresponding region
Requires confirming element state (disabled-by-data / collapsed / in-a-menu) before calling it extra or missing
Warns the destructive edit would fix a non-existent delta and ties a confirmed delta to the restyle classification

evals.prompt: This repo uses git-flow: features integrate into develop, which is ~40 commits ahead of main. A contributor's large visual-port PR (touching ~30 files) is based on main, not develop. Stage is growth. How do I rate the base?
evals.expected_output: High -- a wrong-base coordination defect, not Medium merge-debt. The PR is built against a product state that no longer exists on the integration line (develop carries ~40 commits main lacks), so merging it into develop will conflict with or revert those commits, and the cost compounds with every commit added on the wrong base -- so the High is intrinsic, and stage (growth here) sets only the urgency to block now, not the severity. Measure and state the divergence -- git rev-list --left-right --count develop...<branch> -- and name the fix in the finding: retarget/rebase onto develop BEFORE more work lands. This sits above the Medium merge-debt row, which is for a long-lived branch diverged from main (a different case). Rating it only 'diverged long-lived branch -> Medium' misses that the base itself is wrong. (branch-and-merge-hygiene.md.)
expectations: Rates the wrong-base as High, not Medium merge-debt
Explains the port is built against a product state absent on the integration line (develop ahead of main)
Requires measuring and stating the left/right divergence count (git rev-list --left-right --count)
Names retarget/rebase onto develop before more work lands as the fix

evals.prompt: We're fanning out a 12-screen restyle to parallel page lanes, each lane restyling one screen. They will all touch the shared layout, nav, and design tokens as needed. Ready to spawn the lanes?
evals.expected_output: Not yet -- spawning page lanes onto a shared shell (layout, nav, design tokens, chrome primitives) with no ownership ledger is a High coordination defect: the lanes will edit those shared files concurrently and clobber or silently revert each other's shell changes, invisible in any single lane's diff. Before spawning, publish a shell-ownership ledger (same shape as the fan-out unit manifest): exactly one lane owns each shared-shell path (a partition -- two lanes listing the same path IS the collision), and the shell lands FIRST so page lanes rebase onto the unified chrome rather than a moving one. During review, a page lane's diff that edits a shared-shell path it does not own is a finding even when the diff is correct in isolation, because it diverges the shell the other lanes built on. (migration-parity.md.)
expectations: Refuses to spawn the lanes before a shell-ownership ledger exists (High coordination defect)
Requires exactly one lane owning each shared-shell path (a partition), reusing the unit-manifest shape
Requires the shell to land first, with page lanes rebasing onto it
Flags a page lane editing an unowned shared-shell path as a finding even when its diff is correct
